clinical_category: Joint replacement - recognition of surgical/prosthetic joint infection
blueprint_topic: Infection-prevention teaching and early recognition of postoperative infection
stem: A client is preparing for discharge after total joint replacement. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding of infection-related follow-up?

options.A: I will promptly report increasing redness or pain around the incision, cloudy or new wound drainage, increasing joint swelling or persistent worsening pain, or fever because these may indicate infection.
options.B: Drainage and increasing redness are expected during recovery, so I should wait until the joint becomes unusable before contacting the surgical team.
options.C: Once the incision is closed, an implanted joint can no longer become infected, so infection monitoring is needed only in the hospital.
options.D: Persistent joint pain after replacement rules out infection because prosthetic joint infection always causes a high fever before other symptoms appear.

rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies redness and pain around a surgical site, cloudy wound drainage, and fever as warning findings of surgical site infection, including infections involving implanted material such as a hip replacement. AAOS patient guidance on joint-replacement infection also emphasizes early recognition of incision redness, joint swelling, persistent pain and other infection findings because prosthetic joint infection can require substantial additional treatment. B delays evaluation of concerning wound changes. C is incorrect because prosthetic joint infections can occur after hospital discharge and may present later. D is incorrect because infection does not require a high fever to be present before local or pain-related findings become clinically important. The final item focuses on source-supported postoperative recognition and escalation rather than bundling multiple perioperative prophylaxis protocols into one answer.
educational_objective: Teach clients after joint replacement to recognize and promptly report wound or joint findings that may indicate surgical or prosthetic joint infection rather than assuming infection risk ends at discharge or requires high fever.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS)
source_document_title: Surgical Site Infection Basics; Infection After Joint Replacement
source_version_date: CDC SSI Basics updated 2024-04-11 and current; current AAOS OrthoInfo joint-replacement-infection resource accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: CDC 'Surgical Site Infection Basics' → Overview/Types: SSI can involve implanted material such as a hip replacement; Signs and symptoms: redness and pain around the surgical area, cloudy wound drainage and fever. AAOS OrthoInfo 'Infection After Joint Replacement' → early-recognition guidance: watch for redness at the incision, joint swelling and persistent pain; long-term follow-up is important because some infections can emerge or recur later.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC and AAOS sources directly support recognition and prompt reporting of local wound/joint and systemic findings compatible with infection after joint replacement and establish that implanted material can be involved in SSI.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p. 8 (PDF pageno 11) and Appendix A printed p. 24 (PDF pageno 27): apply principles of infection prevention and educate clients/staff regarding infection-prevention measures; protect clients from health and environmental hazards.
correction_summary: Total rebuild. The source answer bundled antibiotic timing, sterile technique and ongoing monitoring under a generic AAOS citation. The final version narrows the construct to directly source-supported postoperative infection recognition and reporting, preserving Safety and Infection Prevention and Control while eliminating protocol-specific prophylaxis claims that lacked one precise current locator.
audit_findings: The original item combined several perioperative infection-prevention strategies and cited only a generic AAOS source, making exact claim support unnecessarily diffuse.
Fresh CDC review directly supports wound redness/pain, cloudy drainage and fever as SSI findings and explicitly includes implanted material such as hip replacements.

Current AAOS patient guidance independently supports early recognition of incision redness, joint swelling and persistent pain in prosthetic-joint infection and ongoing follow-up beyond the hospital stay.
Distractors test delayed reporting, false end-of-risk after incision closure and high-fever-only assumptions; none is defensible.

Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct discharge-teaching statement with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, unsupported antibiotic-timing rule, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
